Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
235 AM EST Wed Nov 11 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 234 AM EST Wednesday...

Forecast snow totals have increased in the higher elevations for 
Thursday into Friday.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 234 AM EST Wednesday...

1. Increased confidence in impactful elevation-dependent 
snowfall Thursday into Friday. 

2. Lingering upslope rain/snow showers possible on Sunday, 
followed by much quieter and warmer weather next week. 
 
&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 234 AM EST Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A gradually deepening surface low will track from the 
Ohio Valley east over southern New England before heading off into 
the Canadian Maritimes on Thursday into Friday. Despite a favorable 
storm track for snow, a marginally cold initial airmass will be in 
place at the onset, especially at the surface due to a lack of 
Canadian high pressure to the north. Precipitation looks to enter 
southwestern areas Thursday morning but very slowly make its way 
northeast during the day. By Thursday night, it should reach the 
Northeast Kingdom, but the heaviest rates may remain to the south. 
At the onset, surface temperatures will likely be in the 30s in most 
places, with low 40s possible in the warmest valleys. Steep lapse 
rates will exist with summit levels well below freezing, though a 
lack of a significantly dry layer will prevent significant wet-bulb 
cooling. 

Precipitation will begin as rain in the valleys and snow at the 
summits. A first estimate of initial snow levels is around 1,500 ft. 
Light rates and daytime occurrence will prevent significant 
accumulations at the onset outside the mountains. A weak November 
sun angle will limit some of the warming effects though. Heading 
into Thursday night, heavier rates will likely enter the region, and 
darkness will end any solar radiation. The combination of lowering 
temperatures due to dynamical cooling and nighttime cooling will 
allow snow levels to drop a bit, and especially allow for more 
efficient accumulations at higher elevations with higher snow 
ratios. By Friday morning, snow levels should be around or below 
1,000 ft. While brief periods of snow are possible in the low 
valleys like the Champlain Valley and Lower Connecticut Valley, 
temperatures may stay just above freezing and prevent accumulations 
other than some slush in grassy-type surfaces. 

As the low tracks to the east heading through Friday, cyclonic 
northwest flow will develop and maintain some upslope snow showers 
in the higher terrain into Saturday. Boundary layer temperatures 
will reach their lowest values Saturday morning, with most areas 
likely seeing temperatures in the 20s. Warm Lake Champlain 
temperatures will probably further limit the already marginal 
accumulations in the immediate Champlain Valley, especially with 
northwest flow off the lake and downsloping along the eastern 
Adirondacks. 

Overall, this is still a relatively low-confidence forecast. Our 
deterministic most-likely scenario has snow amounts in the 3-6 inch 
range for areas around and above 2,000 ft. One exception is northern 
Vermont, where the heaviest bands may not reach. Areas between 1,000-
2,000 ft look to be in the 1-3 inch range, and below 1,000 ft looks 
to be a slushy coating. However, the ensemble spread is still 
massive. The NBM 10th percentile is 2-4 inches above 2,000 ft and 
the 90th percentile is 10-18 inches. Deterministic models are all 
split. This is mostly due to QPF differences and not 
temperatures/ratios so any significant accumulations in the lower 
elevations like the Champlain Valley are unlikely at this point. 

In higher end scenarios, there would be a power outage threat in the 
higher elevations. The snow will be a heavier, wetter snow, prone to 
sticking to trees and powerlines. It may end a bit drier with lower 
ratios in the Adirondacks if enough cooling occurs on the backside, 
but the exact details remain to be seen.

KEY MESSAGE 2: The cyclonic upslope flow from departing low pres wl 
produce a few light rain and mtn snow showers on Sunday, along with 
plenty of clouds. A building ridge of high pres both aloft and at 
the sfc is progged to expand acrs the Great Lakes/NE CONUS by next 
week. This wl result in much drier atmospheric profiles, with pw 
values btwn 0.20 and 0.40" by early next week. As 1035mb high pres 
builds directly overhead, expect large daily swings in temps from 
cool night-time lows to mild day-time highs, given the dry airmass 
and nightly inversions. No significant or impactful wx is 
anticipated for days 4 thru 7. Highs generally mid 40s to lower 50s 
and lows mid 20s to mid 30s.

&&

.AVIATION /06Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Through 06Z Thursday...Current radar indicates scattered showers
continue to impact the region with a combination of MVFR and VFR
conditions. Given upslope flow thinking MVFR cigs prevail at
MPV/SLK and EFK with intervals of MVFR at RUT/MPV, while mostly
VFR is expected at MSS/PBG thru 12z this morning. Winds continue
from the northwest at 5 to 10 knots. As moisture near the
surface slowly dissipates, expect cigs to trend toward VFR at
all sites by 16z today with northwest winds prevailing. These
conditions continue into Weds evening. 

Outlook...

Thursday: Mainly MVFR, with areas IFR possible. Definite RA,
Definite SN.
Thursday Night: Mainly IFR, with local MVFR possible. Likely RA,
Likely SN.
Friday: Mainly IFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance RA, Chance
SN.
Friday Night: MVFR/IFR conditions possible. Chance SHSN, Chance
SHRA.
Saturday: MVFR. Chance SHRA, Chance SHSN.
Saturday Night: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Chance
SHRA, Chance SHSN.
Sunday: Mainly MVFR, with local VFR possible. Chance SHSN, Slight
chance SHRA.
